parsed.summary: This paper investigates the generalization gap in dermatology AI models, focusing on the effects of skin tone and disease distribution shifts. Using public datasets and free-tier compute, the study finds that disease-distribution shift is a larger driver of performance degradation than skin tone. The authors also demonstrate that starting with a dermatology-pretrained foundation model allows for effective adaptation with minimal labeled data.

chk_problem.value: Dermatology AI models trained on light-skinned, cancer-focused datasets underperform in resource-constrained settings with different skin tones and disease distributions.
chk_problem.paper_quote: Dermatology artificial intelligence (AI) models are trained predominantly on light-skinned, cancer-focused image collections, yet are increasingly proposed for deployment in resource-constrained settings (RCS) whose patients differ from the training population along two confounded axes at once: skin tone and disease distribution.

chk_method.value: Evaluated four models as frozen feature extractors on tone-stratified and disease-shifted datasets using linear probing, label-free representation analysis, and low-compute adaptation.
chk_method.paper_quote: We evaluate a cancer-trained baseline (ResNet-50 fine-tuned on HAM10000 and ISIC 2019), two open dermatology foundation models (DermLIP, MONET), and a general-purpose vision model (DINOv3) as frozen feature extractors, probing them on a tone-stratified but disease-matched dataset (Diverse Dermatology Images, DDI) and a disease-shifted, tone-diverse dataset (Skin Condition Image Network, SCIN).

chk_data.value: Used HAM10000 and ISIC 2019 as in-domain datasets, DDI for tone-stratified evaluation, and SCIN for disease-distribution shift analysis.
chk_data.paper_quote: We use four public datasets, each assigned a specific experimental role (Table 1).

chk_setup.value: Extracted frozen embeddings from four models and evaluated them using linear probing, label-free representation quality, and low-compute adaptation on public datasets.
chk_setup.paper_quote: For each (model, dataset) pair we extract frozen embeddings and evaluate with three analyses.

chk_primary_result.value: Cancer baseline degrades from 0.62 to 0.21 balanced accuracy on SCIN, while the DDI tone gap is smaller (0.10-0.18) and inconsistent in direction.
chk_primary_result.paper_quote: The cancer baseline is strong in-domain (0.62) but degrades sharply on unfamiliar conditions (0.21 across categories; 0.06 at fine granularity).

chk_secondary_result.value: Dermatology foundation models retain more transferable structure, with DermLIP achieving +0.23 kNN neighbor-purity lift over chance on SCIN.
chk_secondary_result.paper_quote: Dermatology foundation models retain three to four times more transferable structure under the same unfamiliar conditions (DermLIP +0.23), and the general-vision control also exceeds the cancer baseline.

chk_baseline.value: Cancer baseline (ResNet-50 fine-tuned on HAM10000 and ISIC 2019) compared against dermatology foundation models (DermLIP, MONET) and a general-purpose vision model (DINOv3).
chk_baseline.paper_quote: We evaluate a cancer-trained baseline (ResNet-50 fine-tuned on HAM10000 and ISIC 2019), two open dermatology foundation models (DermLIP, MONET), and a general-purpose vision model (DINOv3) as frozen feature extractors.

chk_conclusion.value: Disease-distribution shift is the dominant driver of the generalization gap, and starting with a dermatology-pretrained foundation model allows effective adaptation with minimal labeled data.
chk_conclusion.paper_quote: Using only public data and free-tier compute, we decomposed the dermatology-AI generalization gap and found disease-distribution shift to dominate skin tone, traced the effect to a representational deficit in cancer-specialized models, and found that cheap adaptation is most effective when the starting representation already encodes the target conditions.

chk_limitation.value: DDI and SCIN are US-sourced proxies, and the study does not validate findings on genuinely RCS-collected cohorts.
chk_limitation.paper_quote: First and most importantly, DDI and SCIN are US-sourced proxies used to isolate each factor, not RCS-collected data; our RCS conclusions are therefore inferential, and validation on genuinely RCS-collected cohorts is important future work.
